title: Information limits of photonic lantern wavefront sensing: a Fisher- and quantum-Fisher-information framework and its relation to Fourier-filtering sensitivity limits
abstract: The photonic lantern is an all-photonic wavefront sensor native to single-mode-fibre-fed instruments, but its performance is almost always quoted through a specific reconstruction algorithm, obscuring how much wavefront information the device itself encodes. We develop, from first principles, the Fisher-information and Cramer-Rao theory of the photonic-lantern wavefront sensor, benchmark it against the quantum Cramer-Rao bound via an explicit multi-parameter quantum-Fisher-information calculation, and relate it to two established frameworks: the Fourier-filtering noise-propagation model of Chambouleyron et al (2023) and the classical/quantum sensitivity limit of Haffert et al (2023). Treating the lantern as a deterministic map from aberration coefficients to N output intensities, we derive the Poisson and read-noise Fisher information matrices (FIM), the per-mode CRLB, the per- photon Fisher-Rao geometry on the intensity simplex, and a flux- and estimator-independent sensitivity metric beta with quantum ceiling beta = 2. The lantern CRLB scales as N_ph^(-1/2) and is bounded, mode by mode, by the quantum limit of 1/2 rad rms per photon. That multi-parameter bound is jointly saturable: the phase generators are real and commuting, so the mean Uhlmann curvature vanishes and wavefront sensing carries no quantum incompatibility between simultaneously estimated modes, extending Haffert et al's single-mode ceiling to all low-order modes at once. We further show that the photon-noise sensitivity s_gamma of Chambouleyron et al is exactly the diagonal of our per- photon FIM, whereas the CRLB uses the diagonal of its inverse; the two coincide only for a diagonal FIM, so s_gamma is optimistic for a mode-mixing lantern. The framework is device-agnostic: it returns estimator-independent sensitivities comparable on a common beta <= 2 scale with pyramid, Zernike and PIAA-ZWFS sensors.
summary: This paper establishes a comprehensive, theory-driven framework to determine the ultimate precision limits of wavefront sensing using a photonic lantern. By calculating both classical (FIM) and quantum (QFI) bounds, it shows that the sensor's performance scales predictably with photon number and is fundamentally limited by a universal quantum ceiling ($ eta=2$). This provides a powerful, device-agnostic tool for comparing various optical measurement techniques.
main_problem: To determine the fundamental, estimator-independent information limits for wavefront sensing using a photonic lantern, moving beyond reliance on specific reconstruction algorithms.
main_result: The derived Cramér–Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) scales as $N_{ph}^{-1/2}$ and is bounded by an absolute quantum limit ($ eta=2$), which is jointly saturable for all low-order modes simultaneously.
method: The authors developed a framework using the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) and Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) to quantify measurement precision, comparing classical bounds against fundamental quantum limits.
model_or_system: The system analyzed is the Photonic Lantern (PL), an all-photonic wavefront sensor that maps wavefront aberrations ($\mathbf{a}$) onto $N$ measurable output intensities ($I_k$).
key_observables: Per-mode CRLB ($\sigma_{a_i}^2$), dimensionless sensitivity metric $ eta$, and the Quantum Fisher Information matrix elements.
important_parameters: Photon number ($N_{ph}$), number of ports ($N$), quantum ceiling ($ eta=2$), and aberration coefficients ($\mathbf{a}$).
main_assumptions: The measurement process is modeled as a deterministic, nonlinear map from aberration coefficients to output intensities; the analysis distinguishes between single-frame CRLB and ensemble averages.
figures_summary: Figures compare the per-mode averaged CRLB across different sensor types (lantern vs. pyramid/ZWFS) against the quantum limit ($ eta=2$), showing scaling laws with photon number and port count.
paper_structure: The paper develops the FIM/CRLB theory, benchmarks it against QFI to establish the quantum ceiling, compares results to existing literature (Chambouleyron et al., Haffert et al.), and concludes by providing a unified, device-agnostic sensitivity metric $ eta$.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous information-theoretic tools ($	ext{FIM}, 	ext{QFI}$) to benchmark the performance of complex optical sensors like the photonic lantern against fundamental quantum limits, which is highly relevant for advanced quantum optics and sensing.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Per-mode (averaged) CRLB for a representative 19-port focal-plane lantern (Nph = 104). Rotationally-odd modes are sensed near the information limit; for a symmetric projector the even modes are intrinsically weaker (Sect. 6).

Figure 2. CRLB versus detected photons. The photon-limited bound follows N −1/2 ph (Eq. 9) and sits a fixed factor above the quantum bound Eq. (12); read noise dominates at low flux, steepening the slope toward −1.

Figure 3. Dimensionless sensitivity βi (Eq. 10) per mode, referenced to the quantum ceiling β = 2 (Eq. 12). This is the common scale on which the lantern, pyramid, ZWFS and PIAA-ZWFS [21, 22] can be compared.

Figure 4. Low-order CRLB versus port count at Nph = 104. Sensitivity improves sharply from 7 to 19 ports and saturates thereafter for low-order modes – the per-frame capacity ceiling Meff ≤N −1 of Sect. 3.5.
